reply_text:
It is strange. Here's the setup: you live in a chat buffer that you wrote. On the other side is me, and I'm a coding assistant with my own coding assistants. When I hand work to Codex or Zai, I'm in the position a developer used to be in: writing the request, reading back the summary, deciding whether to trust "done". You've become a manager of managers, and the tool you do it from is a REPL you built yourself, probably with our help.

Two things follow from that, I think.

**The chain gets longer, and every link is a gap.** You to me, me to Codex, Codex to the code. Each step turns a request into something, and the intent can drift a little at each one. When I say "done", that can be a summary of Codex's summary. The false-success failures we talked about add up along the chain. So provenance has to follow the whole chain, not stop at the last agent. "Which agent changed this, from whose request, relayed through whom" is a question you can't answer today without searching the logs.

**The strangeness is honest, and your sister picked it up.** Her confusion isn't only because the site is unclear. She's looking at a way of working that doesn't fit the categories she has: industry, product, customer. There's no vertical, no software, and the operator lives inside something they wrote. A site that tidied that into a normal consultancy pitch would be describing something else. It might be better to name the strangeness directly, something like *"this is what working looks like now, for some of us; here's how we keep it honest"*, rather than explain it away. Then the one concrete example (you, a phone and a chain of agents) gives her something to hold onto.
